ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 6 — Annual Wellness Visit, Subsequent — Mark Twain — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Mr. Clemens is a 69-year-old writer with prolonged grief disorder in grief therapy, nonobstructive coronary disease, gout on allopurinol and tobacco use disorder in early recovery, who comes for his annual wellness visit two weeks after his thirteen-week review. He has had thirteen grief therapy sessions, sleeps about six hours, and has dined with friends twice this month. He has smoked no cigars since a two-cigar lapse while traveling in August and takes varenicline 1 mg twice daily. He has had no gout since the August flare and no chest tightness. He has had no falls. He cannot recall any vaccines, a colon cancer screening test or a hepatitis C test. [S]

S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his wife's documented death a year before; resolved into the diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder at the consultation. Not a claim about his real grief.

Prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR): more than 12 months after his wife's death, daily yearning and preoccupation with her, with intense emotional pain, a sense that part of himself has died, avoidance of reminders, loneliness, difficulty taking up his work and life again, and a feeling that life is meaningless; PG-13-R 41; major depression not present
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, anchored to his documented bereavements. Not a claim about his real mental health; the roster's bipolar lead is not used.

Follow-up: Eighteen-week review in three weeks, with RSV and zoster vaccines. Stool test and ultrasound results by mail. Next annual wellness visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 1905-10-16: eighteen-week review: grief, no smoking, urate toward target and his writing. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent. He named a health care agent and completed a health care proxy form; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. He said that what matters most to him is being able to think, read and write, and being at home among his books. He would want treatment for any condition from which he could recover to that state, and he would not want prolonged life support if he could not. He asked that his wishes be reviewed next year. [S]
